elements.char: Abstract
elements.label: text

elements.char: Self-organization in the cell relies on the rapid and specific binding of molecules to their cog-
elements.label: text

elements.char: nate targets. Correct bindings must be stable enough to promote the desired function even
elements.label: text

elements.char: in the crowded and fluctuating cellular environment. In systems with many nearly matched
elements.label: text

elements.char: targets, rapid and stringent formation of stable products is challenging. Mechanisms that
elements.label: text

elements.char: overcome this challenge have been previously proposed, including separating the process
elements.label: text

elements.char: into multiple stages; however, how particular
elements.label: text

elements.char: in vivo
elements.label: text

elements.char: systems overcome the challenge
elements.label: text

elements.char: remains unclear. Here we consider a kinetic system, inspired by homology dependent pair-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ing between double stranded DNA in bacteria. By considering a simplified tractable model,
elements.label: text

elements.char: we identify different homology testing stages that naturally occur in the system. In particular,
elements.label: text

elements.char: we first model dsDNA molecules as short rigid rods containing periodically spaced binding
elements.label: text

elements.char: sites. The interaction begins when the centers of two rods collide at a random angle. For
elements.label: text

elements.char: most collision angles, the interaction energy is weak because only a few binding sites near
elements.label: text

elements.char: the collision point contribute significantly to the binding energy. We show that most incorrect
elements.label: text

elements.char: pairings are rapidly rejected at this stage. In rare cases, the two rods enter a second stage
elements.label: text

elements.char: by rotating into parallel alignment. While rotation increases the stability of matched and
elements.label: text

elements.char: nearly matched pairings, subsequent rotational fluctuations reduce kinetic trapping. Finally,
elements.label: text

elements.char: in vivo chromosome are much longer than the persistence length of dsDNA, so we extended
elements.label: text

elements.char: the model to include multiple parallel collisions between long dsDNA molecules, and find
elements.label: text

elements.char: that those additional interactions can greatly accelerate the searching.

elements.char: Author summary
elements.label: text

elements.char: Protein folding and the binding of sequence dependent proteins to DNA are examples of
elements.label: text

elements.char: self-assembling systems in which the binding energy varies continuously throughout the
elements.label: text

elements.char: interaction. Previous theoretical work has highlighted the importance of dividing the
elements.label: text

elements.char: interaction into separate stages characterized by interaction times and binding energies
elements.label: text

elements.char: that vary by orders of magnitude. Insight into how such a division might naturally arise
elements.label: text

elements.char: and promote accurate and efficient self-assembly is provided by our study of a simple trac-
elements.label: text

elements.char: table model inspired by the homology dependent pairing of double stranded DNA mole-
elements.label: text

elements.char: cules in vivo. In the model, the binding energy is controlled by one single continuously
